'''Sekazi Kauze Mtingwa''':<ref name="mitreview">{{Cite web|url=https://www.technologyreview.com/s/603455/sekazi-k-mtingwa-71/|title=Sekazi Mtingwa works to help underrepresented minorities succeed in STEM fields|last=Waugh|first=Alice|website=MIT Technology Review|access-date=2019-03-04}}</ref> (born '''Michael Von Sawyer''';<ref name="aipinterview">{{Cite web|url=https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/44300|title="Sekazi Mtingwa {{!}} American Institute of Physics"}}</ref> October 20, 1949) is an American theoretical [[particle physics|high-energy]] physicist. He is a co-recipient of the 2017 Robert R. Wilson Prize for Achievement in the Physics of Particle Accelerators.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Mtingwa&first_nm=Sekazi&year=2017|title=2017 APS Prize Recipient|website=www.aps.org|access-date=2019-03-04}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Mtingwa&first_nm=Sekazi&year=2017|title=2017 Robert R. Wilson Prize for Achievement in the Physics of Particle Accelerators Recipient|website=www.aps.org|access-date=2019-03-04}}</ref> He is the first African-American to be awarded the prize.<ref name="mitreview" /> Mtingwa was elected a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] (APS) <ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.thehistorymakers.org/biography/sekazi-mtingwa|title=Sekazi Mtingwa's Biography|website=The HistoryMakers|access-date=2019-03-04}}</ref> in 2008 for "his definitive treatment of Intrabeam scattering, his contributions to the wakefield acceleration, and his early recognition of the fixed target physics potential of the next generation electron-positron collider."<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=www.aps.org|access-date=2019-03-04}}</ref> He also co-founded the [[National Society of Black Physicists]] in 1977 <ref name=":1" />  and served in various other national and international initiatives.

== Early life and education ==
Mtingwa was born in Atlanta, Georgia on October 20, 1949. His father was a Lockheed assembly line worker, and his mother was a nurse's assistant.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|date=2020-06-02|title=Sekazi Mtingwa|url=https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/44300|access-date=2021-06-18|website=www.aip.org|language=en}}</ref>

He attended segregated schools until 10th grade. In that year, the Georgia State Science Fair was integrated, and Mtingwa won first place in biology. He was the first African-American to win.<ref name=":4" /> His prize included books in science, mathematics, and engineering, including three books on Einstein's theory of special relativity, which inspired him to pursue physics as a career.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|title=Sekazi K. Mtingwa '71|url=https://www.technologyreview.com/2017/02/22/5465/sekazi-k-mtingwa-71/|access-date=2021-06-18|website=MIT Technology Review|language=en}}</ref>

He studied physics and pure mathematics at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT), where he received B.S. degrees in both subjects in 1971. While an undergraduate, he helped found the Interphase EDGE (then Project Interphase) program to prepare incoming students in subjects such as physics and math. He was also involved in the student protests of the late 1960s.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Zierler |first=David |date=March 27, 2020 |title=Oral history interview with Sekazi Mtingwa, 2020 March 27. |url=https://libserv.aip.org/ipac20/ipac.jsp?session=15U110795R1E7.12811&profile=rev-icos&uri=full%3D3100006~%2144300~%210&ri=3&menu=search&source=~%21horizon |website=nsf.gov}}</ref> Afterwards, he joined graduate school at [[Princeton University]], where he earned a Ph. D. degree in theoretical high energy physics in 1976.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|date=2018-10-20|title=Sekazi Mtingwa|journal=Physics Today|doi=10.1063/PT.6.6.20181020a|s2cid=239919564 }}</ref> The title of his PhD thesis is "Asymptotic chiral invariance and its consequences,"<ref>{{cite thesis |id={{ProQuest|302772312}} |last1=Mtingwa |first1=Sekazi Kauze |year=1976 |title=Asymptotic Chiral Invariance And Its Consequences }}</ref> which he completed under the supervision of [[Curtis Callan]].<ref name=":4" /> While in graduate school, he changed his name from Michael Von Sawyer to Sekazi Kauze Mtingwa, a [[Tanzania]]n name.<ref name="aipinterview" />

== Career ==
After graduating from [[Princeton]], Mtingwa took a research associate position, which turned into a part-time assistant professorship including some teaching duties, from [[Susumu Okubo]] at the [[University of Rochester]].<ref name="aipinterview" /> There in Rochester, Mtingwa met and soon married Estella Johnson.<ref name="mitreview" /><ref name="aipinterview" /> In 1978, he took a post-doctoral research position at the [[University of Maryland, College Park]] in the Center for Theoretical Physics.

Mtingwa received a [[Ford Foundation]] fellowship in 1980 and took it to [[Fermilab]] in [[Illinois]] for a one-year postdoctoral position, and became a research physicist there in 1981.<ref name="aipinterview" /> In joint work with [[James Bjorken]], an American theoretical physicist who is Emeritus Professor at the [[Stanford Linear Accelerator Center]], he developed a theory of "[[intrabeam scattering]]" in particle accelerators.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bjorken |first1=James D. |last2=Mtingwa |first2=Sekazi K. |year=1983 |title=Intrabeam scattering |journal=Particle Accelerators |volume=13 |issue=3–4 |pages=115–143 |url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/140304/files/p115.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kubo |first1=Kiyoshi |last2=Mtingwa |first2=Sekazi K. |last3=Wolski |first3=Andrzej |title=Intrabeam scattering formulas for high energy beams |journal=Physical Review Special Topics - Accelerators and Beams |date=12 August 2005 |volume=8 |issue=8 |article-number=081001 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevSTAB.8.081001 |bibcode=2005PhRvS...8h1001K |doi-access=free }}</ref> 
<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Piwinski |first1=Anton |last2=Bjorken |first2=James D. |last3=Mtingwa |first3=Sekazi K. |title=Wilson Prize article: Reflections on our experiences with developing the theory of intrabeam scattering |journal=Physical Review Special Topics - Accelerators and Beams |date=7 November 2018 |volume=21 |issue=11 |article-number=114801 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevAccelBeams.21.114801 |bibcode=2018PhRvS..21k4801P |doi-access=free |hdl=1721.1/119136 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> For this work, he was awarded the 2017 Robert R. Wilson Prize for Achievement in the Physics of Particle Accelerators,<ref name=":0" /> since that theory ''"empowered major discoveries in a broad range of disciplines by a wide variety of accelerators, including hadron colliders, damping rings/linear colliders, and low emittance synchrotron light sources.''"<ref name=":0" />

While at Fermilab, he also contributed in a significant way to two of the antiproton source accelerator systems,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Church |first1=M D |last2=Marriner |first2=J P |title=The Antiproton Sources: Design and Operation |journal=[[Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science]] |date=December 1993 |volume=43 |issue=1 |pages=253–295 |doi=10.1146/annurev.ns.43.120193.001345|bibcode=1993ARNPS..43..253C | doi-access=free }}</ref> which were instrumental in particle discoveries, including that of the [[top quark]].

In 1988–1991, Mtingwa worked at [[Argonne National Laboratory]], where he developed theory of advanced wakefield and plasma acceleration <ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mtingwa |first1=Sekazi K. |title=Theory of the anisotropic ferrite wake-field accelerator. I. Azimuthally symmetric case |journal=Physical Review A |date=1 May 1991 |volume=43 |issue=10 |pages=5581–5589 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.43.5581 |pmid=9904871 |bibcode=1991PhRvA..43.5581M |doi-access= }}</ref> and of the photon colliders.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mtingwa |first1=Sekazi K. |last2=Strikman |first2=Mark |title=B factory via conversion of 1-TeV electron beams into 1-TeV photon beams |journal=Physical Review Letters |date=26 March 1990 |volume=64 |issue=13 |pages=1522–1525 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.64.1522 |pmid=10041419 |bibcode=1990PhRvL..64.1522M |doi-access=free }}</ref> Starting in 1991, he joined the faculty at North Carolina A&T State University as Chair and Professors of Physics (with a brief stint at Morgan State University in 1997–1999). From 2001 to 2003, he was a visiting professor of physics at MIT, followed by two years as a visiting professor of physics at Harvard University. He returned to MIT in 2006.<ref name=":1" /> He retired in 2012 and has since focused on outreach efforts.<ref name=":5" />

He is a Fellow of the American Physical Society (elected in 2008)<ref name=":2" /> and of the American Association for the Advancement of Science (elected in 2015<ref>{{cite journal |title=AAAS Members Elected as Fellows |journal=Science |date=27 November 2015 |volume=350 |issue=6264 |pages=1047–1049 |doi=10.1126/science.350.6264.1047 |doi-access=free }}</ref>).
